common_name: Dark Dude Louisiana Iris (Near-Black Velvety Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Dark Dude was bred by Louisiana hybridizer Ron Betzer from 'Bout Midnight' x 'Margaret Lee' and carries standards so deeply saturated with red-black pigment that they read almost as true black, paired with velvety black falls and a contrasting gold dagger signal. It went on to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal, the top national award for the species, and is prized by Gulf South gardeners for adding dramatic near-black contrast to bright bayou-iris plantings. Give it consistently moist to wet soil and full sun for the darkest color saturation, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to keep bloom vigorous.

common_name: Lemon Zest Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Lemon-Green Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Hybridized by Kevin Vaughn from 'Heavenly Glow' x 'Vermilion Queen', Lemon Zest opens bright lemon yellow and ages to a softer creamy lemon, with an electric green signal area and heavily ruffled, lightly serrated form that sets it apart from older yellow Louisianas. It blooms earlier than most cultivars in its class and earned the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal for its combination of vigor and unusual coloring. Site it in full sun with steady moisture, since the cool green tones intensify when the rhizomes never dry out between waterings.

common_name: Seminole Sunrise Louisiana Iris (Yellow and Cardinal Red Bitone)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Bred by Florida hybridizer Harry Wolford from 'All Agaze' x 'Red Echo', Seminole Sunrise carries yellow standards that blend into dark pink at the edges above cardinal red falls, an unusually vivid bitone that earned it the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal. The warm color combination reads especially well against the blue and purple Louisianas that dominate most bayou-iris collections. Keep the clump in full sun and shallow standing water or reliably moist soil through bloom season for the strongest color contrast.

common_name: Deja Voodoo Louisiana Iris (Deep Purple Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: New Orleans hybridizer Patrick O'Connor introduced Deja Voodoo from 'German Coast' x 'Henry Rowlan', producing a lightly ruffled, deep purple self set off by a bright yellow arrowhead signal on the falls. It won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal and is one of several award-winning dark Louisianas bred specifically for New Orleans-area growing conditions. Grow it in full sun with rich, constantly moist soil, and expect the deep purple tone to hold well even in the humid heat of a Gulf South spring.

common_name: Our Friend Dick Louisiana Iris (Pink-Violet and Dark Violet Bitone)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Texas hybridizer Ron Killingsworth named this tall bitone, bred from 'Dural Bluebird' x 'Hush Money', for a fellow iris enthusiast; the darker-veined pink violet standards sit above dark violet falls with a white halo and golden steeple signal. Its height and vigor helped it earn the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal, and it remains a strong back-of-border choice for bog gardens and pond edges. Give it full sun and steady moisture and expect one of the taller flower stalks among modern Louisiana cultivars.

common_name: Blue Mountain Mist Louisiana Iris (Pale Sky Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Bred by Australian-American hybridizer Bernard Pryor from 'C'est La Mote' x 'Swirling Waters', Blue Mountain Mist bears pale sky blue standards and falls with a fine white rim, ice blue style arms, and a slightly fragrant golden-orange steeple signal. The cultivar collected trial-garden honors on two continents before winning the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in the United States. Plant it in full sun with consistently wet soil, where its soft powder-blue color pairs well against darker purple and red Louisiana cultivars.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Harry Wolford bred Edna Claunch from 'Atchafalaya' x 'Dural White Butterfly', producing lemon-lime standards and falls veined in a deeper lime green with a fine matching signal line. It went on to win both the Marie Caillet Cup from the Society for Louisiana Irises and the national Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal. Its compact size makes it a good fit for smaller water gardens; grow it in full sun with shallow standing water or continuously moist soil for best flowering.

common_name: Peaches In Wine Louisiana Iris (Peach and Deep Red Bitone)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Heather Pryor's early-blooming Peaches In Wine, from 'Bushfire Moon' x 'Lucy Payens', pairs peach-toned standards against deep red falls rimmed in salmon peach, with a lime-yellow steeple signal that glows against the darker color. First recognized in Australian regional trials, it later earned the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in the United States. Grow it in full sun and rich, constantly wet soil, and expect bloom to open earlier in the season than most Louisiana cultivars.

common_name: Hot And Spicy Louisiana Iris (Tomato Red Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Heather Pryor bred Hot And Spicy from 'Gladiator's Gift' x 'Desert Jewel', producing a heavily ruffled tomato-red self with a fine yellow rim and a raised yellow steeple signal surrounded by a matching dagger pattern. Recognized first in Australian trial gardens, it went on to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal for its intense, saturated red color. Full sun brings out the deepest red tones, and the plant tolerates the wet, humid conditions of Gulf Coast bayou gardens especially well.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Mary Dunn's Extraordinaire traces back through 'Blue Shield', 'Black Widow', 'Full Eclipse', and 'Clara Goula' to produce ruffled, serrate flowers in an unusual metallic purple with lime green signals. The complex pedigree and striking sheen helped it win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal, and it remains a benchmark for metallic coloring in Louisiana iris breeding. Plant in full sun with steady moisture; the metallic effect is most visible on flowers that open in cooler, humid spring mornings.

common_name: Great White Hope Louisiana Iris (Tall Near-Black Purple Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Despite its name, Dorman Haymon's Great White Hope is one of the darkest Louisiana irises available, with dark blue-violet standards and near-black, cream-edged falls on some of the tallest flower stalks in the class. Bred from 'Jeri' x 'Easter Tide', it can rebloom in warmer zones such as Texas and went on to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal. Give it full sun, wet feet, and staking room at the back of a bog planting, since the stalks tower well above most companion Louisianas.

common_name: Cajun Sunrise Louisiana Iris (Red and Yellow Sunburst Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Bred by LSU researcher Joseph Mertzweiller from a complex line that includes 'Bayou Sunset', 'Peggy Mac', and 'Upstart', Cajun Sunrise carries red standards edged in narrow yellow above red falls that flare into a bright yellow sunburst pattern near the signal. The cultivar earned the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal and helped anchor a run of red-and-yellow bitone breeding that followed in later decades. Grow it in full sun with continuously moist to wet soil, where the sunburst pattern shows best on flowers opening in early midseason.

common_name: When Pigs Fly Louisiana Iris (Pale Amber Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Patrick O'Connor bred When Pigs Fly from 'Percolator' x 'Bellocq'; the flowers open pale amber and fade to a soft pearl white, with a deep yellow dagger signal outlined in bright violet radiating across much of the fall. The whimsically named cultivar went on to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal for its unusual soft color shift and bold signal pattern. Site it in full sun with rich, wet soil, and watch the color soften noticeably as each bloom ages over several days.

common_name: Eyes Wide Open Louisiana Iris (Creamy White and Cyclamen Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: One of Heather Pryor's most recent introductions, Eyes Wide Open shows creamy white standards blushed with cyclamen pink above medium cyclamen-pink falls rimmed in white, with a large yellow signal outlined by fine red eyeliner and a sweet fragrance rare among Louisiana cultivars. It was awarded the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal, the Society for Louisiana Irises' top national honor. Grow it in full sun with steady moisture, and site it where the fragrance can be appreciated near a patio, deck, or pond-side path.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Hooker Nichols bred Watermelon Wizard from 'Heather Pryor' x 'Guessing Game', producing a salmon-raspberry color blend deepened by darker veining and lines across both standards and falls, with a small gold-line signal. The cultivar collected the Franklin Cook Cup and a Favorite Guest award at Society for Louisiana Irises conventions before winning the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal. Plant it in full sun with consistently wet soil for the strongest expression of its unusual watermelon-toned color blend.
